name: Vector
tagline: Electrify your fleet without the guesswork
description: Vector helps logistics companies plan and execute fleet electrification with confidence. From route-level energy modeling to charging infrastructure placement, we turn the messy EV transition into a phased, data-driven rollout that actually pencils out.
mission:
Every major logistics company has an electrification target on paper. Almost none of them have a credible plan to get there. The gap between commitment and execution is enormous — fleet managers face a maze of vehicle options, charging infrastructure decisions, utility rate structures, and route constraints that make the transition feel impossibly complex.

Vector was built to close that gap. We model every route in your fleet against real-world EV performance data — accounting for payload, terrain, weather, and charging availability — to produce a phased electrification roadmap that maximizes ROI at each stage. No more pilot programs that stall after five trucks.

Our founding team spent years at fleet management companies watching electrification initiatives die in spreadsheet purgatory. The technology exists to make fleets electric. What's missing is an intelligent planning layer that tells you which vehicles to replace first, where to put chargers, how to negotiate utility rates, and when the economics flip in your favor.

We're starting with regional delivery fleets in the 50-500 vehicle range — large enough to benefit from structured planning, small enough to move quickly. Our first customers are saving an average of $12,000 per vehicle annually once they transition, and our planning tool cuts the typical 18-month analysis phase down to weeks.
marketResearch:
The commercial fleet electrification market is expected to reach $180B globally by 2030, with fleet management software for EVs representing an $8.5B addressable market. North American medium-duty delivery fleets — our beachhead — account for roughly $2.3B of that. Our initial SOM targets regional carriers and last-mile delivery companies with 50-500 vehicles, representing $380M in near-term software spend.

Competitors fall into two camps: legacy fleet management platforms (Geotab, Samsara) adding EV modules as afterthoughts, and pure-play EV analytics startups (Electriphi, acquired by Ford; Amply Power) focused narrowly on charging management. Vector differentiates by owning the full planning lifecycle — from route-level feasibility analysis through infrastructure deployment to ongoing optimization. We don't just tell you if EVs will work; we tell you exactly which trucks to replace, in what order, and how to finance it.

Our go-to-market starts with direct sales to fleet operations directors at regional carriers, supported by partnerships with EV OEMs (BrightDrop, Rivian Commercial) who bundle our planning tool with vehicle purchases. Early traction includes 8 paid pilots across beverage distribution and parcel delivery, with an average contract value of $45K annually.

Key tailwinds include the EPA's 2027 emissions standards, state-level fleet electrification mandates (California's Advanced Clean Fleets rule), and rapidly declining battery costs. The window for planning tools is now — fleets that wait will face charger installation backlogs and miss incentive deadlines.

name: Anchor
tagline: Commercial leases shouldn't require a legal team to manage
description: Anchor is a lease management platform for growing companies navigating commercial real estate. We centralize lease data, automate critical date tracking, and surface cost-saving opportunities hidden in your portfolio — so your ops team stops drowning in PDFs.
mission:
Growing companies sign commercial leases the way most people sign gym memberships — with optimism and very little ongoing attention. Then renewal deadlines sneak up, escalation clauses kick in unnoticed, and CAM reconciliations arrive as incomprehensible spreadsheets. By the time anyone realizes there was a problem, the leverage is gone.

Anchor exists because we watched this pattern repeat at every company we worked at. The CFO finds out about an auto-renewal two weeks too late. The ops manager discovers they've been overpaying common area maintenance for three years. The head of real estate keeps critical dates in a personal calendar that nobody else can access.

We're building the system of record for commercial leases that growing companies actually deserve. Not enterprise software designed for REITs with 500-person real estate teams, but a focused tool that extracts the critical data from your leases, tracks every deadline, benchmarks your rates against market data, and flags when it's time to negotiate or exit.

Our long-term play is to become the intelligence layer between tenants and their real estate decisions. When you're ready to expand, Anchor already knows your lease terms, your space utilization patterns, and the market conditions in your target cities. The best real estate decision is an informed one, and right now most growing companies are flying blind.
marketResearch:
The commercial real estate technology market is projected to hit $35B by 2030, with lease management and administration software growing at 12% CAGR. The new ASC 842 and IFRS 16 lease accounting standards have forced every company with material lease obligations to digitize — creating a $4.2B market for lease management tools.

The competitive landscape is dominated by enterprise players: LeaseAccelerator (acquired by Eptura), Visual Lease, and CoStar's lease management tools. These platforms are built for large real estate portfolios and come with 6-figure implementation costs and 3-month onboarding timelines. On the lower end, companies use spreadsheets, shared drives, and calendar reminders — a $0 solution that costs them thousands in missed deadlines and overpayments.

Anchor targets the gap: companies with 3-50 commercial leases who need professional lease management without enterprise overhead. This represents approximately $900M in addressable spend across 180,000 mid-market companies in North America. Our initial SOM focuses on Series B+ startups and mid-market companies in tech, professional services, and healthcare — roughly $150M.

Our PLG motion starts with free lease extraction: upload a PDF, get structured lease data in minutes. Teams upgrade when they need critical date alerts, portfolio analytics, and ASC 842 compliance reporting. We partner with commercial brokers who recommend Anchor to their tenant clients, creating a referral flywheel.

name: Silo
tagline: Pick faster. Walk less. Ship more.
description: Silo optimizes warehouse slotting — the art of deciding where every SKU lives on the shelf. By analyzing order patterns, pick sequences, and velocity data, we rearrange your warehouse so pickers walk less and throughput climbs. No racking changes required.
mission:
In most warehouses, products end up where they end up. Fast movers sit in the back because that's where they were put during the last big receiving day. Slow movers hog prime pick slots because nobody reassigned them when demand shifted. The result: pickers walk miles of unnecessary distance every shift, and throughput hits a ceiling that no amount of overtime can fix.

Silo was born in a 200,000 square foot fulfillment center where we watched pickers average 8.3 miles per shift — not because the warehouse was large, but because it was badly slotted. We ran a manual reslotting project that took six weeks of analysis and cut pick time by 22%. Then demand patterns changed two months later and we were back to square one.

That experience made one thing clear: warehouse slotting isn't a project, it's a continuous optimization problem. Silo treats it that way. We ingest your WMS data, analyze order co-occurrence patterns, velocity curves, and physical constraints, then generate reslotting recommendations that your team can execute in waves — no forklift rodeo required.

We're not replacing your WMS. We're making the one you have dramatically more effective by ensuring every item lives in the right place at the right time. Our customers see 15-30% pick time reductions within the first reslotting wave, and the gains compound as Silo continuously adapts to shifting demand.
marketResearch:
The warehouse management systems market is projected to reach $11.1B by 2030, with optimization add-ons like slotting, labor planning, and simulation tools growing at 15% CAGR. The slotting optimization niche specifically represents approximately $1.8B in addressable spend. Our SAM — mid-market fulfillment operations in North America running pick-pack-ship workflows — is roughly $520M. Our initial SOM targets direct-to-consumer e-commerce fulfillment centers and 3PLs with 50K-500K square feet, representing $85M.

Competitors include built-in slotting modules from WMS vendors (Manhattan Associates, Blue Yonder) that require expensive licenses and consultant-led implementations, standalone tools like Optricity (acquired by Honeywell) that focus on enterprise distribution centers, and homegrown spreadsheet-based approaches used by 70%+ of mid-market warehouses. Silo wins by being WMS-agnostic, fast to deploy (days, not months), and continuously adaptive rather than project-based.

Our GTM strategy targets operations managers and warehouse directors through content marketing around pick efficiency metrics, partnerships with 3PL technology consultants, and a free slotting audit that analyzes WMS data exports to quantify improvement potential. Early customers convert from the free audit at 40%, with average contracts of $2,800/month for a single facility.

name: Waypoint
tagline: Last-mile delivery that stops burning money on wrong turns
description: Waypoint optimizes last-mile delivery routes in real time, balancing delivery windows, driver capacity, traffic patterns, and fuel costs. Built for regional delivery fleets that need enterprise-grade routing without enterprise-grade budgets.
mission:
Last-mile delivery is the most expensive, most chaotic, and most customer-visible part of the supply chain. A single bad routing decision cascades — late deliveries, angry customers, exhausted drivers, and margins that evaporate with every extra mile driven.

Waypoint was founded by a team that ran delivery operations for a regional grocery chain and lived through the daily chaos firsthand. Dispatchers using Google Maps and tribal knowledge to plan 200 deliveries across 30 drivers. Routes built on assumptions from last Tuesday's traffic. Delivery windows missed because nobody accounted for a school zone on Third Street.

We built the routing engine we wished we'd had: one that ingests real-time traffic, historical delivery times, customer time windows, vehicle capacity, and driver hours-of-service constraints — then produces routes that are genuinely optimal, not just directionally correct. And it does this in minutes, not the hours it takes a human dispatcher.

Our vision is simple: every regional delivery fleet should have access to the same routing intelligence that Amazon and FedEx spend billions developing in-house. The technology isn't the hard part anymore. The hard part was making it accessible, affordable, and fast enough for a dispatcher to use at 5am before the trucks roll out.
marketResearch:
The route optimization software market is valued at $7.4B and growing at 11.2% CAGR, driven by e-commerce growth and rising fuel costs. The last-mile segment specifically represents $3.1B of this market. Our SAM focuses on regional delivery fleets in North America — grocery, beverage, building materials, and home services — with 10-200 vehicles, representing roughly $850M. Our SOM targets the eastern US corridor, approximately $140M.

The competitive field includes enterprise platforms (Descartes, ORTEC, PTV Group) with complex implementations and six-figure annual costs, mid-market tools (OptimoRoute, Routific, Route4Me) with varying levels of sophistication, and free tools (Google Maps, Circuit) that lack multi-constraint optimization. Waypoint positions between mid-market and enterprise: real optimization that handles complex constraints (time windows, vehicle types, driver skills, live traffic) at a price point mid-market fleets can absorb.

Our differentiation is speed and accuracy in constrained environments. Most competitors optimize for distance; Waypoint optimizes for total delivery cost including fuel, labor, failed delivery penalties, and customer satisfaction scores. Our engine produces routes in under 90 seconds for 500-stop problems, versus 10-30 minutes for comparable solutions.

GTM strategy combines content marketing targeting fleet operations managers with partnerships with fleet management platforms (Fleetio, Azuga) and delivery management software providers. Free tier handles up to 50 stops/day, converting to paid plans for multi-driver, multi-depot operations.

name: Cornerstone
tagline: Run your coworking space like a business, not a hobby
description: Cornerstone is a management platform purpose-built for coworking and flex space operators. Billing, member management, room booking, access control, and community tools — unified in one system instead of duct-taped across seven.
mission:
The coworking industry has exploded, but the tools haven't kept up. Most operators run their spaces on a Frankenstein stack — Stripe for billing, Google Calendar for room bookings, a spreadsheet for member tracking, and a physical keycard system that nobody bothers to update. The result: manual work that scales linearly with membership, billing errors that erode trust, and zero visibility into what's actually working.

Cornerstone was built by operators, for operators. Our founding team ran three coworking spaces in Austin and spent more time wrestling with software than building community. We tried every platform on the market — some handled billing well but had terrible booking. Others had nice member portals but couldn't manage multi-location operations. None of them talked to our access control system.

We decided to build the platform we couldn't find: a single system that handles the entire coworking operation from first tour to monthly invoice. Member lifecycle management, automated billing with flexible plan structures, room and desk booking with real-time availability, access control integration, community features, and the analytics operators need to make smart decisions about pricing and space utilization.

Our north star is freeing operators to focus on what actually differentiates their space: the community, the experience, and the programming. The back-office shouldn't eat your day.
marketResearch:
The global coworking space market is projected to reach $40B by 2030, growing at 15% CAGR. The management software segment supporting this market represents approximately $2.8B in TAM. Our SAM focuses on independent coworking operators and small chains (1-20 locations) in North America and Europe, representing $780M. Our SOM targets single-location and small multi-location operators in the US, roughly $120M.

The competitive landscape includes Optix (strong mobile experience, weak on billing complexity), OfficeRnD (good feature breadth, dated UX), Nexudus (European market leader, complex to configure), and Cobot (developer-friendly but limited scaling). Enterprise flex operators use in-house solutions or platforms like Yardi/MRI that aren't coworking-native. Cornerstone differentiates through operational simplicity — a single platform that covers billing, booking, access control, and community without requiring a technical co-founder to configure.

Our GTM is community-led, starting with coworking operator communities (GWA, GCUC conferences) and content marketing around operational benchmarks. We offer a free tier for spaces under 25 members, converting to paid plans as spaces grow. Average contract value is $350/month for a single location, scaling to $1,200/month for multi-location operators. Our biggest growth lever is the access control integration — once a space's door locks run through Cornerstone, switching costs become significant.

name: Manifest
tagline: Stop overpaying on freight. Start auditing automatically.
description: Manifest automates freight bill auditing and payment for shippers who are tired of overpaying carriers. We catch billing errors, duplicate charges, and contract non-compliance that manual processes miss — then handle payment so your AP team can focus on literally anything else.
mission:
Freight invoices are wrong more often than most shippers realize. Industry studies put the error rate between 5-15%, but in our experience it's often higher. Duplicate charges, incorrect accessorial fees, weight discrepancies, fuel surcharge miscalculations, and rates that don't match contracted terms. Multiply that by thousands of shipments per month and you're bleeding money you'll never recover.

Manifest started because our founder spent a decade in logistics finance and watched companies hire entire teams just to check invoices against contracts — a process that's tedious, error-prone, and always behind. The worst part: even the best manual audit catches maybe 60% of errors. The other 40% gets paid without question.

We built an engine that ingests every freight invoice, matches it against your carrier contracts and shipment records, flags discrepancies with specific dollar amounts and root causes, and either auto-approves clean invoices or routes exceptions to your team with all the context they need to resolve them. No more spreadsheet reconciliation. No more paying invoices on faith.

But auditing is just the entry point. Our vision is to become the financial intelligence layer for freight operations — helping shippers understand their true landed cost per shipment, identify carrier performance trends, and negotiate better contracts with data they've never had access to before.
marketResearch:
The freight audit and payment market is valued at $3.2B globally, growing at 9% CAGR as supply chains digitize and shipping volumes increase. The North American segment represents $1.4B, with mid-market shippers (500-50,000 shipments/month) being the most underserved — too large for manual processes, too small for enterprise solutions like Cass Information Systems or nVision Global.

Our SAM targets mid-market manufacturers, distributors, and retailers shipping via LTL, TL, and parcel in North America — approximately $480M in addressable spend. Our initial SOM focuses on companies with $5M-$100M in annual freight spend, representing roughly $80M.

Competitors include legacy freight payment companies (Cass, CTSI-Global) with lengthy implementations and outdated technology, newer platforms (Loop, Shipwell's audit features) with narrower scope, and in-house AP teams using spreadsheets and manual processes. Manifest differentiates through automation depth — we don't just flag errors, we identify root causes, calculate recovery amounts, and generate carrier dispute documentation automatically.

Our GTM strategy starts with a free freight audit on 90 days of historical invoices — showing shippers exactly how much they've been overpaying before they commit. This creates a powerful conversion moment. Average savings identified in the free audit: $47K. Paid plans charge a percentage of recovered savings in year one, transitioning to flat monthly pricing, aligning our incentives with customer value.

tagline: Property management that doesn't require a property manager
description: Domicile is built for small landlords managing 1-20 rental units who need professional-grade tools without the overhead. Rent collection, maintenance coordination, tenant screening, and accounting — all in one place, designed for people who have a day job.
mission:
There are 11 million individual landlords in the United States, and most of them manage their properties with a combination of Venmo, text messages, and a shoebox of receipts. They're not real estate professionals — they're teachers, engineers, and small business owners who own a duplex or a handful of rental units as an investment. And the software industry has mostly ignored them.

Enterprise property management platforms like Yardi and AppFolio are designed for professional management companies with hundreds of units and dedicated office staff. They're powerful, expensive, and wildly over-engineered for someone managing four apartments. On the other end, tools like Cozy (now Apartments.com) have been hollowed out or absorbed into platforms that prioritize listing revenue over landlord experience.

Domicile fills this gap with genuine care for the small landlord. We automate the operational burden — rent collection with automatic late fees and receipts, maintenance requests that tenants submit through the app instead of 11pm text messages, lease management with e-signatures, and accounting that generates Schedule E tax reports without a bookkeeper.

We believe small landlords provide essential housing in communities across America, and they deserve tools that respect their time and intelligence. Not dumbed-down versions of enterprise software, and not consumer apps that treat property management as an afterthought.
marketResearch:
The US residential property management software market is $3.4B, growing at 8% CAGR. However, the small landlord segment (1-20 units) represents 70% of all rental units nationally but only 15% of software spend — a massive underserved opportunity estimated at $1.2B. Our SAM targets individual landlords and small LLCs in the US with 1-20 units, approximately $680M. Our SOM focuses on digitally-savvy landlords in the top 50 metro areas, roughly $110M.

The competitive landscape: Buildium and AppFolio serve the 50-500 unit professional segment. TurboTenant and Avail target small landlords but are primarily tenant screening and listing tools with property management bolted on. Stessa handles financials well but lacks operational features. Domicile differentiates by being the only purpose-built, full-stack platform for the small landlord — combining the operational tools of enterprise platforms with the simplicity that part-time landlords need.

Our freemium model offers free rent collection (monetized via optional tenant-paid ACH fees) and upgrades to $12/unit/month for the full suite including maintenance management, accounting, document storage, and tax reporting. This pricing is 60-80% below AppFolio or Buildium on a per-unit basis.

GTM strategy leverages content marketing targeting real estate investing communities (BiggerPockets, Reddit r/landlord), partnerships with real estate investment education platforms, and a referral program that gives landlords a free month per referral. Our CAC is $38, with LTV of $1,400 based on average 3.2-year retention and 6.8 units per account.

name: Berth
tagline: Port scheduling that actually keeps ships moving
description: Berth optimizes dock and port scheduling for maritime terminals, reducing vessel wait times and maximizing berth utilization. We replace the whiteboards, phone calls, and spreadsheets that most ports still use to manage the most expensive parking spots on earth.
mission:
A single container vessel sitting idle at anchor costs between $30,000 and $80,000 per day. Multiply that by the dozens of ships waiting outside every major port and you start to understand the scale of the scheduling problem in maritime logistics. Ports are the critical bottleneck in global trade, and most of them still coordinate berth assignments with phone calls, emails, and whiteboards.

Berth was founded by a team with deep roots in port operations who saw this inefficiency from the inside. The problem isn't that port operators lack skill — it's that they lack tools. A modern container terminal juggles vessel arrivals, tide windows, crane availability, berth depth restrictions, cargo type compatibility, and labor scheduling simultaneously. Doing this in spreadsheets means decisions are reactive instead of optimized.

We built a scheduling engine purpose-built for the unique constraints of port operations. Berth considers vessel dimensions, draft requirements, cargo handling equipment, terminal operating system data, tide tables, and weather forecasts to produce berth schedules that maximize throughput while minimizing vessel wait times.

Our initial focus is mid-size ports and private terminals that lack the IT budgets of mega-ports like Rotterdam or Shanghai but face the same scheduling complexity. These are the ports where a 15% improvement in berth utilization means the difference between profitability and requesting government subsidies.
marketResearch:
The port management software market is projected to reach $6.8B by 2030, with berth scheduling and terminal optimization representing approximately $1.9B. The global shift toward port digitization — driven by congestion crises, emissions regulations, and vessel size increases — is accelerating adoption. Our SAM targets mid-size container and bulk terminals in North America, Europe, and Southeast Asia, roughly $520M. Our initial SOM focuses on US and Canadian ports with 200K-2M TEU annual throughput, approximately $65M.

Competitors include terminal operating system (TOS) vendors like Navis (Cargotec) and TBA Group that offer berth planning as modules within larger systems, standalone optimization tools from companies like INFORM and PortLink, and in-house Excel-based systems used by 60%+ of mid-size ports. Berth differentiates through standalone deployment (no TOS replacement required), real-time optimization that adapts to disruptions, and a modern UX that operations teams can actually use without weeks of training.

Our GTM strategy targets port operations directors and terminal managers through industry conferences (TOC, AAPA), partnerships with maritime consultancies, and a free simulation tool that lets ports model their current operations and see optimization potential before committing. Sales cycles are 3-6 months with average contract values of $120K-$400K annually depending on terminal size.

Key market tailwinds: the IMO's 2030 carbon intensity targets are pushing ports to reduce idle time (less fuel burned at anchor), chassis and container dwell time regulations in California, and the trend toward port automation that requires digital scheduling as a foundation layer.

name: Threshold
tagline: Your building is wasting energy. We can see exactly where.
description: Threshold is a smart building energy management platform that connects to existing BMS and IoT sensors to identify waste, automate savings, and help commercial buildings hit sustainability targets — without replacing any hardware.
mission:
Commercial buildings consume 35% of all electricity in the United States, and studies consistently show that 20-30% of that energy is wasted. HVAC systems heat empty floors. Lights burn in unoccupied conference rooms. Chillers run at full capacity when outdoor air could do the job. The waste isn't from bad equipment — it's from dumb controls and zero visibility.

Threshold exists because we believe every commercial building already has the data it needs to cut energy costs dramatically. The BMS has temperature readings. The meters have consumption data. The access control system knows which floors are occupied. The problem is that these systems don't talk to each other, and nobody is watching the patterns at 2am when the real waste happens.

We connect to the systems your building already has — BACnet BMS, smart meters, occupancy sensors, weather feeds — and layer on intelligence that identifies waste patterns, automates setpoint adjustments, and surfaces the changes that will save the most money with the least disruption. No new hardware. No construction. Just software that makes your existing building perform like it was designed to.

Our team comes from the intersection of building science and machine learning. We've operated buildings, designed HVAC systems, and built the models that predict when a chiller is about to fail. Threshold is the tool we wish we'd had: one that turns building data into action without requiring a PhD in mechanical engineering.
marketResearch:
The smart building energy management market is projected to hit $15.3B by 2030, growing at 14% CAGR. Key drivers include ESG reporting mandates (EU CSRD, SEC climate disclosure rules), rising energy costs, and local building performance standards (NYC LL97, Boston BERDO). The compliance pressure alone is creating $4.2B in demand for energy optimization software.

Our SAM targets commercial office buildings, retail portfolios, and institutional campuses (100K-2M sqft) in North America — approximately $2.1B. Our SOM focuses on buildings in cities with active building performance standards, roughly $340M.

Competitors include large building analytics platforms (75F, acquired by Johnson Controls; Cohesion, BuildingIQ) that require significant hardware investment, point solutions for HVAC optimization (Brainbox AI, Parity) with narrower scope, and legacy BMS vendors (Honeywell, Siemens) adding analytics as premium modules. Threshold differentiates by being hardware-agnostic, software-only, and focused on delivering ROI through operational changes rather than capital projects.

Our GTM targets building operations directors and sustainability managers through building industry associations (BOMA, IFMA), energy consultancy partnerships, and content marketing around building performance standards compliance. Free energy audits analyzing 90 days of meter data create a strong conversion funnel — average identified savings of $1.40/sqft/year against a platform cost of $0.25/sqft/year makes the ROI case straightforward.

name: Cartage
tagline: The freight marketplace where shippers and carriers actually find each other
description: Cartage is a digital freight marketplace that connects shippers with vetted carriers for LTL, FTL, and drayage loads. Transparent pricing, real-time tracking, and none of the phone tag that makes freight brokerage feel stuck in 1995.
mission:
Shipping freight in America is a $900 billion industry that still runs on phone calls, faxes, and relationships. A shipper with a load to move calls their broker. The broker calls five carriers. Three don't answer. One quotes too high. One can do it but not until Thursday. An hour later, a truck is booked at whatever price emerged from this chaotic process. Repeat 50 times a day.

Cartage was founded because we believe freight matching should work like every other marketplace in 2026 — transparent, instant, and data-driven. Shippers post loads with origin, destination, commodity, and timing. Carriers see loads that match their lanes, equipment, and availability. Pricing is informed by real market data, not whatever the broker feels like quoting.

But we're not naive about why brokers exist. They provide trust, credit, and problem-solving that a simple load board can't replace. So we built Cartage to capture the best parts of brokerage — carrier vetting, payment guarantees, and exception management — while eliminating the worst parts: opacity, phone tag, and the 15-20% margin that ultimately comes out of both sides' pockets.

Our long-term play is building the freight operating system for mid-market shippers. Marketplace access today, freight analytics tomorrow, and eventually, automated procurement that dynamically routes loads across carriers based on cost, reliability, and capacity — without a human broker in the middle.
marketResearch:
The US freight brokerage market generates $90B+ annually, with digital freight brokerages growing at 25% CAGR as shippers demand transparency and carriers seek to fill empty miles. The total addressable market for digital freight matching platforms is approximately $18B. Our SAM targets mid-market shippers ($1M-$50M annual freight spend) and carriers with 5-200 trucks in the US, representing roughly $5.2B. Our SOM focuses on the eastern US LTL and FTL market, approximately $800M.

Competitors include digital freight brokerages (Convoy — paused operations, Uber Freight — scaling back, Loadsmart) that have struggled with unit economics, traditional brokerages going digital (CH Robinson's Navisphere, Echo Global), and load boards (DAT, Truckstop) that offer matching without transaction services. Cartage differentiates by operating as a true two-sided marketplace with transparent pricing — not a digital brokerage that still takes a hidden spread. Our 8% take rate versus the industry's 15-20% margin creates a structural cost advantage.

Our GTM strategy starts with lane density in the I-95 corridor where we can offer reliable carrier coverage. Shippers join through a free RFQ tool that benchmarks their current rates against market data. Carriers are acquired through an app that shows available loads with guaranteed payment terms. Network effects kick in as lane density increases: more carriers means better pricing, which attracts more shippers.

Key market tailwinds: broker fee transparency regulations under consideration, carrier consolidation creating more digitally-savvy fleets, and rising shipper demand for real-time visibility that traditional brokers can't provide.
